High-level answer (summary) — will draft a short matrix and attach spreadsheet.

1) GPU recommendation- For SUSTAINED 120 req/s (avg 600 tokens/request) with low-latency targets, our tests show H100 (80GB) single-GPU model variants handle ~20-30 concurrent generation streams for large models with kv-cache friendly configs. For safety and operational simplicity: start with a pool composed of H100 80GB (or A100 80GB where H100 unavailable) and target the following:
  - Baseline pool: 8 x H100 (80GB) -> provides sustained headroom for 120 req/s with 35% margin for typical 7B-13B model variants trimmed for latency
  - Burst capacity: add 4 extra GPUs as hot-spare/burst nodes (scales via pre-warmed instances) to reach 380 req/s bursts

2) Autoscale policy (private)
  - Warm pool approach: keep a minimum pool of 70% capacity always online. During expected traffic windows, spin up up to +30% as warm spare nodes (these are started but warmed).
  - Fast-burst: maintain 4 pre-allocated hot nodes (GPU instances started, runtime warmed, KV caches primed) that can accept traffic immediately. Use policy: if CPU/GPU util > 65% for 30s then shift traffic to hot nodes and trigger allocator to attach more.

3) Warmup & KV-cache strategy  - Pre-population: for chat-style workloads, pre-execute the top 200 prompt prefixes collected from production telemetry across the hot nodes to populate KV cache and compilation caches.
  - Rolling deploys: deploy incrementally across nodes and run the warmup script against newly deployed nodes before adding to live routing.
  - Cache TTLs: set KV cache TTLs to at least 1 hour during peak windows; on failover, prioritize nodes that have been recently warmed.

4) Networking notes  - NIC: 100Gbps NIC recommended for host machines when running 8+ GPUs to avoid RPC bottlenecks.
  - MTU: enable jumbo frames (MTU 9000) where possible for NVLink/RDMA-backed traffic.
  - NAT/egress: prefer dedicated egress IPs per deployment to simplify firewall rules and avoid ephemeral NAT exhaustion.

I’ll attach a draft capacity-matrix with projected token/sec numbers per GPU and expected p95 latencies. Will also produce a 1-page warmup script (bash) for the customer.

Quick notes to the plan:
- Margin: I recommend we size for 40% headroom instead of 35% because StellarAI’s traffic is bursty and they’re latency-sensitive.
- Availability: plan for cross-AZ node placement (2 AZs) with even distribution to avoid AZ-correlated failure. Keep at least 1 hot node in each AZ.
- Egress routing: for private installs that use NAT gateways, we see transient connection loss during NAT scaling events; recommend using dedicated NAT instances or assign EIPs to critical control-plane endpoints.
- Security: ensure the warmup script runs over a private management channel (not public internet) and signs requests with the customer’s API key.

I’ll update the spreadsheet with 40% margin numbers and AZ placement.

Observability + runbook bullets:
- Metrics to monitor: per-GPU generation QPS, per-request latency p50/p95/p99, KV cache hit rate, model compilation failures, load-balancer queue depth, NIC tx/rx util, socket errors.
- Alarms: p95 latency > 400ms for 2 minutes, KV cache hit rate < 70% for 5 mins, GPU util > 90% for 5 mins.
- Runbook snippet:
  1) After deploy, run cache-warmup-script.sh against each new node. Verify KV cache hit rate > 85% on warm nodes before routing traffic.
  2) If unexplained p95 spikes occur, fail traffic to hot spare nodes, then investigate compilation logs and disk I/O.
  3) For AZ failover, adjust routing weight to remaining AZ then spin up replacement nodes in the failed AZ; do not rely on autoscaler alone during incident.
